UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                    BEFORE THE
                      FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

AEP Generation Resources Inc.                            )                     Docket No. EC26-153-000
Longview Power, LLC                                      )

                   RESPONSE OF APPLICANTS TO THE COMMENTS OF
                    THE INDEPENDENT MARKET MONITOR FOR PJM

        Pursuant to Rule 385.213(a)(3) of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s

(“Commission” or “FERC”) Rules of Practice and Procedure, 1 AEP Generation Resources Inc.

(“GenResources” or the “Buyer”) and Longview Power, LLC (“Longview”) (referred to

collectively with GenResources as the “Applicants”) hereby respond to the Comments of the

Independent Market Monitor (“IMM”) for PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (“PJM”) filed in this

docket on October 16, 2026 (“IMM Comments”). 2 For the reasons discussed below, the

criticisms by the IMM of the Commission’s approach to market power analysis under section

203 of the Federal Power Act (“FPA”) and the IMM’s recommended market behavior conditions

should be rejected, and the application filed by Applicants pursuant to section 203 of the FPA

(“Application”)3 should be approved.


1

Applicants seek leave to file this response. Although the Commission’s procedural rules do not allow for answers to

England Inc., 181 FERC ¶ 61,260 at P 11 (2022); PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 181 FERC ¶ 61,162 at P 29 (2022),
modified, 184 FERC ¶ 61,006 (2023), aff’d sub nom. Hecate Energy LLC v. FERC, 126 F.4th 660 (D.C. Cir. 2025).
The Commission accepted answers to the IMM’s substantially similar comments in Docket Nos. EC26-81-000 and
EC26-82-000 “because they have provided information that assisted us in our decision-making process.” AEP
Generation Res. Inc., 196 FERC ¶ 61,081 at P 24 (2026) (“Wolf Hills/Big Sandy Order”).
2
  Comments of the Independent Market Monitor for PJM, Docket No. EC26-153-000 (Oct. 16, 2026) (“IMM
Comments”). The market power report attached to the IMM Comments as Attachment A-1 is referred to herein as
the “IMM Report.”
3
  Joint Application for Authorization of Transaction under Section 203 of the Federal Power Act and Requests for
Waivers of Filing Requirements and Confidential Treatment, Docket No. EC26-153-000 (Aug. 17, 2026)
(“Application”).



                                                       -1-
 I.         BACKGROUND

           On August 17, 2026, Applicants filed the Application requesting the Commission to

authorize a transaction pursuant to which Mountain State Energy Holdings, LLC (the “Seller”)

would sell to GenResources 100% of the equity interests in Longview (the “Transaction”).

Longview owns an approximately 710 MW (summer rating) coal-fired generating facility

located in Maidsville, West Virginia. The Application included an affidavit, exhibits, and

workpapers prepared by Julie Solomon and Jeffrey Opgrand of Secretariat LLC (“the

Solomon/Opgrand Affidavit”) demonstrating, among other things, that the transaction will not

have an adverse effect on competition in any relevant wholesale electricity market. 4 The

Commission noticed the filing of the Application on August 18, 2026, with a comment deadline

of October 16, 2026.5 On October 16, 2026, the IMM filed the IMM Comments.

II.        RESPONSE

           The IMM Comments largely repeat, often word for word, the comments the IMM filed

on May 29, 2026 in Docket Nos. EC26-81-000 and EC26-82-000 opposing the acquisitions of

Wolf Hills Energy, LLC (“Wolf Hills”) and Big Sandy Peaker Plant, LLC (“Big Sandy”) by

affiliates of American Electric Power Company, Inc. (“AEP”). 6 On July 30, 2026, the

Commission authorized those transactions and rejected each of the IMM’s arguments. 7 In that

order, the Commission declined to rely on the IMM’s pivotal supplier analyses, found that the

IMM’s alternative analyses were of limited usefulness because they consisted of summary-level

5

this docket. Supplemental Filing, Docket No. EC26-153-000 (Oct. 15, 2026).

 Compare IMM Comments at 3-20 with Comments of the Independent Market Monitor for PJM at 3-18, Docket
Nos. EC26-81-000 and EC26-82-000 (May 29, 2026) (“May 29 IMM Comments”).
7

                                                          -2-
 results without the underlying data, rejected the IMM’s request that the applicants commit not to

remove capacity from the PJM capacity market, and declined to impose the IMM’s seven

proposed behavioral conditions.8 The IMM now urges FERC to impose the same seven

conditions on the same corporate family, supported by the same type of analysis. 9 The IMM

Comments do not acknowledge the Wolf Hills/Big Sandy Order, much less offer any basis for the

Commission to reach a different result here.

           The IMM’s few new arguments fare no better. The IMM now asks the Commission to

apply the 2023 Merger Guidelines issued by the U.S. Department of Justice (“DOJ”) and Federal

Trade Commission (“FTC”) and to evaluate the “accumulated increase in structural market

power” from AEP’s prior acquisitions and from consolidation in PJM generally. 10 But the

Commission has not adopted those guidelines, as the IMM itself acknowledges, and the IMM

recommends that the Commission take up these issues “in a separate rulemaking.” 11 In any

event, the Commission’s established analysis already captures the cumulative effect of AEP’s

prior acquisitions, and that analysis shows that the relevant markets remain unconcentrated after

the Transaction. As in the Wolf Hills/Big Sandy Order, the IMM’s recommendations should be

rejected and the Application should be approved.

           A.      The Transaction Is Consistent with the Public Interest.

           As demonstrated in the Application, the Transaction is consistent with the public interest.

The Commission reviews three factors when evaluating proposed transactions under the section

203 public interest standard: (i) the effect on competition; (ii) the effect on rates; and (iii) the


8
    Id.
9
 Compare IMM Comments at 19-20 with May 29 IMM Comments at 16-18; see Wolf Hills/Big Sandy Order at P
39 (summarizing the seven conditions).
10
     IMM Comments at 2-3 & n.8, 6 & n.18.
11
     IMM Report at 12-13.



                                                  -3-
 effect on regulation.12 Applicants have shown that the Transaction (i) will not have an adverse

effect on competition, (ii) will not have an adverse effect on rates, and (iii) will not have an

adverse effect on regulation.13 The Application also demonstrates that the Transaction will not

result in cross-subsidization or the pledge or encumbrance of utility assets. 14

            The IMM argues that Applicants have not asserted that the Transaction provides “any

offsetting public benefits, such as enhanced competition or market efficiency,” and that the

Transaction “cannot be approved, including on balance, without a finding that benefits to the

public interest offset the harm identified in the record.” 15 The Commission rejected this framing

in the Wolf Hills/Big Sandy Order, explaining that “[t]o challenge a proposed transaction, a party

must demonstrate that the proposed transaction will have an adverse effect on horizontal

competition not that a proposed transaction must have some competitive benefit or market

enhancement.”16 As discussed below, the IMM has not demonstrated any such adverse effect.

            B.       The Commission Has Already Rejected the IMM’s Alternative Market
                     Power Analyses, and the IMM’s Renewed Analyses Suffer from the Same
                     Defects.

                     1.         The Transaction Easily Passes the Commission’s Screens.

            The Commission’s rules are explicit in requiring use of the Delivered Price Test (“DPT”)

and an evaluation of market concentration as measured by the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index

(1997).

(1st Cir. 1993)).

 (“HHI”) and the change in that statistic as a result of a transaction. 17 As set forth in the

Solomon/Opgrand Affidavit, the Transaction easily passes these screens. The PJM and PJM

West markets are unconcentrated in all seasons and load periods after the Transaction, and the

HHI changes are no higher than 15 points under the Economic Capacity and Available Economic

Capacity measures at base case prices and under the price sensitivities. 18 Based on installed

capacity, the Transaction increases HHI by only 8 points in PJM and 14 points in PJM West. 19 In

the PJM capacity market, even treating AEP’s Fixed Resource Requirement (“FRR”) capacity as

if it participated in the capacity market, the Transaction increases HHI by only 6 points. 20

            The IMM does not dispute any of these results. To the contrary, the IMM acknowledges

that the DPT “analysis provided by applicants shows no screen failures in the PJM market nor in

the previously established submarkets that include both AEP and Longview generation for which

applicants submitted analysis, which includes the PJM West submarket.” 21 As the Commission

has explained, “an unconcentrated market means that a proposed transaction is unlikely to have

adverse competitive effects.”22

                      2.      The Commission Has Declined to Rely on the IMM’s Pivotal Supplier
                              Analyses.

            Rather than engage with the Commission’s screens, the IMM offers its own alternative

analyses based on hourly market shares, HHIs, and the frequency with which AEP is a pivotal

supplier under a “three pivotal supplier” (“TPS”) test and a “one pivotal supplier” (“OPS”) test,

constraints, and in the PJM capacity market. 23 The IMM submitted the same types of analyses in

the Wolf Hills and Big Sandy proceedings. 24 The Commission declined to rely on them:

           The PJM IMM submitted alternative analyses for the aggregate PJM energy market,
           proposed local energy markets, and the PJM-wide capacity market measuring
           changes by hourly market shares, HHIs, single pivotal supplier frequency and three
           pivotal supplier frequency. However, the Commission has previously explained

           of FPA section 203 transactions and that three pivotal supplier analyses are not
           required from applicants seeking authorization for a proposed transaction under
           FPA section 203. We will not rely on the PJM IMM’s three pivotal supplier test
           results or analysis in this proceeding.25

           Nothing in the IMM Comments warrants a different result here. The only methodological

change is that the IMM now applies an OPS test, in addition to its TPS test, to its proposed local

energy market analysis.26 But the IMM already presented single pivotal supplier results for the

aggregate energy market in the Wolf Hills and Big Sandy proceedings, and the Commission

declined to rely on any of the IMM’s alternative analyses in that proceeding. 27 The IMM’s

assertion that its OPS test “is consistent with the Commission’s pivotal supplier screen used for

Market Based Rates”28 does not make it an appropriate substitute for the Competitive Analysis

Screen that the Commission’s section 203 regulations require. 29

                     3.       The IMM’s Analyses Continue to Lack the Underlying Data Needed
                             to Evaluate Them.

           The Commission also declined to rely on the IMM’s alternative analyses in the Wolf

Hills/Big Sandy Order for an independent reason:

           In addition, all of the PJM IMM’s alternative analyses include summary level data
           and results, lack the underlying data for the Commission to analyze how the
           summary results are developed, or otherwise omit calculations, which limits the
           usefulness of these analyses. Accordingly, we will not rely on the PJM IMM’s
           alternative analyses in this proceeding.30

           The same is true here. The IMM Report again presents its results only as summary tables

of market shares, HHIs, pivotal supplier frequencies, and average TPS and OPS scores. 31 The

IMM has not provided workpapers, the underlying market data, the distribution factors applied to

the generation resources included in its measures of supply, or the calculations by which its

summary results were derived. By contrast, Applicants submitted the workpapers supporting the

Solomon/Opgrand Affidavit.32 The Commission therefore lacks any more basis to rely on the

IMM’s alternative analyses here than it had in the Wolf Hills/Big Sandy Order.

           The IMM asserts that its analysis “has been accepted for consideration in other

Commission proceedings.”33 But consideration is not reliance. In two of the cited orders, the

Commission conditioned approval on settlements that the applicants voluntarily negotiated with

the IMM, while expressly basing its competitive findings on its own analysis. 34 And unlike here,

stated only that, “while applicants must continue to provide a Competitive Analysis Screen, we

competitive analysis and recommended solutions “do not necessarily align with or serve as a surrogate for the
Commission’s analysis”).

                    4.         The IMM Has Not Established the Existence of Any Local
                              Submarket.

            The IMM contends that AEP’s local market power would increase in submarkets defined

by transmission constraints.42 In the Wolf Hills/Big Sandy Order, the Commission found that the

IMM “has not provided adequate support to establish the existence of such separate geographic

markets,” because, “[w]hile the PJM IMM provided information about the identified

transmission constraints, it has failed to provide sufficient information about potential boundaries

for the alleged local markets or submarkets or to explain how the constraints are distinguishable

from existing submarkets in PJM.”43 The Commission also “decline[d] to use the pivotal supplier

test to define or evaluate relevant energy submarkets.”44

            The IMM Comments do not cure these deficiencies. Although the IMM now limits its

local analysis to constraints binding in more than 876 hours over two years, 45 it continues to

define its proposed local markets exclusively through the TPS and OPS tests, which the IMM

describes as defining markets “based on the electricity network, rather than geography.” 46 The

IMM does not identify the boundaries of any proposed submarket, the load or customers within

it, or how any such submarket differs from the PJM West submarket that Applicants analyzed. 47

Nor does the IMM’s bare assertion that “[t]he conditions for requiring a detailed analysis of

submarkets exist” supply the missing support.48 And, as IMM acknowledges, “no submarket

mix, load and transmission expansion” which change the shape of local markets. 49 The relevant

geographic markets for this Transaction remain the PJM market and the PJM West submarket,

and the Transaction raises no concerns in either. 50

                    5.       The IMM’s Own Analyses Do Not Show That the Transaction Raises
                             Market Power Concerns.

           The IMM’s alternative analyses, taken on their own terms, do not support its claim of

competitive harm. As explained in the attached Supplemental Affidavit of Julie R. Solomon and

Jeffrey J. Opgrand, the IMM’s results largely corroborate the Application. 51 The IMM

acknowledges that the Transaction produces no screen failures in the PJM market or the PJM

West submarket,52 and concedes that the increases it identifies “reflect the relatively small size of

the Transaction compared to AEP’s large current position in the market.” 53 The IMM’s objection

is thus to AEP’s existing portfolio, not to any effect of the Transaction. And, as the Supplemental

Affidavit explains, the IMM Report omits the information needed to evaluate its proposed local

markets, including the resources, distribution factors, and market boundaries underlying its

results.54 As in NRG, the IMM has not made “a convincing case that the Proposed Transaction

has anticompetitive effects.”55

                     6.    A Rulemaking Would Be Required to Adopt the IMM’s Preferred
                          Approach.

           What the IMM advocates, as in its comments in prior transactions, is a rewrite of the

Commission’s regulations to replace the Commission’s HHI-based Competitive Analysis Screen

with a pivotal supplier test that the Commission has repeatedly declined to adopt. A rulemaking

proceeding would be required to change the Commission’s regulations to reflect the test the

IMM prefers. The Commission cannot implement such a change in the adjudication of an

individual section 203 application. The IMM invokes the principle that the Commission may not,

“in its quasi-judicial capacity, ignore its own pronouncement promulgated in its quasi-legislative

capacity,” and argues that “[t]he Commission’s rules should be followed.” 56 Applicants agree. In

this case, the Commission’s rules for applications under Section 203 of the FPA should be

followed.57 These rules prescribe the Competitive Analysis Screen, 58 and the Transaction passes

it. Nothing in those rules, or in the Merger Policy Statement, requires the Commission to rely on

an intervenor’s alternative analysis. Rather, intervenors “may file an alternative competitive

analysis accompanied by appropriate data to support their arguments,” and the Commission will

consider such analyses “if adequately supported.” 59

           The IMM’s own report now confirms that the changes it seeks are generic in nature. The

IMM states that “[t]he Commission’s merger policy does not address longer term trends in

concentration or the effect of sequential transactions,” that it “does not define a maximum level

of concentration or a maximum market share that is consistent with competitive outcomes,” and

Commission’s existing regulations govern this Transaction.

            C.       The IMM’s “Series of Acquisitions” and Industry Consolidation Arguments
                     Provide No Basis to Deny or Condition Authorization of the Transaction.

            The IMM argues that the Transaction is “one of a series of AEP acquisitions” and that

“[t]he accumulated increase in structural market power of the multiple transactions should be

evaluated as part of the review of mergers and acquisitions, but it is not taken into account in the

current case by case review process currently used for Section 203 filings.” 61 The IMM relies on

Guideline 8 of the 2023 DOJ/FTC Merger Guidelines, which provides that the agencies may

examine a series of acquisitions as a whole.62 The IMM also points to Guideline 7, concerning

industry trends toward consolidation, to argue that the Commission should consider recent and

pending transactions by other large PJM capacity owners. 63 These arguments fail for three

reasons.

                     1.      The 2023 Merger Guidelines Are Not the Commission’s Standard.

            The Commission evaluates the competitive effects of a proposed transaction under

section 203 using the Merger Policy Statement and the Competitive Analysis Screen codified in

its regulations.64 When DOJ and FTC revised their horizontal merger guidelines in 2010, the

Merger Guidelines”)).

 Commission considered whether to revise its own approach and, after notice and comment,

decided to retain its existing framework. 65 The IMM acknowledges that “[t]he Commission has

not reevaluated and updated its guidelines based on subsequent revisions to the Department of

Justice and Federal Trade Commission’s guidelines.” 66 The 2023 Merger Guidelines therefore do

not supply the standard for this proceeding, and the IMM cannot import them through comments

in an individual section 203 proceeding any more than it can import its pivotal supplier test.

                     2.     The Commission’s Analysis Already Accounts for AEP’s Prior
                            Acquisitions.

            The IMM’s premise that the cumulative effect of AEP’s prior acquisitions “is not taken

into account” is incorrect. Here, the Solomon/Opgrand Affidavit treats AEP’s recent and pending

acquisitions, including Oregon Clean Energy, Big Sandy, and Wolf Hills, as part of AEP’s pre-

Transaction portfolio.67 The post-Transaction HHIs reported in the Solomon/Opgrand Affidavit

therefore reflect the combined effect of all of those acquisitions plus Longview, and the PJM and

PJM West markets remain unconcentrated. 68 In other words, the Commission’s established

screen already does what the IMM says it does not: it evaluates the market structure that results

from the “series” as a whole.

            Moreover, each of AEP’s prior acquisitions identified by the IMM was reviewed and

authorized by the Commission over the IMM’s objections. The Commission authorized the

acquisition of Oregon Clean Energy in 2025. 69 In authorizing the Wolf Hills and Big Sandy

simultaneously” for the purposes of its horizontal market analysis because “this provides a more

conservative approach,” and still found that the transactions would have no adverse effect on

The IMM’s request that the Commission now treat the “accumulated” market power from those

authorized transactions as a harm to be mitigated in this proceeding amounts to an impermissible

collateral attack on those orders.

                    3.      Generalized Concerns About Industry Consolidation Are Beyond the
                            Scope of This Proceeding.

           The IMM’s broader argument about consolidation in PJM, citing recent or pending

transactions involving Constellation, Talen, ArcLight, Vistra, NRG, LS Power, Dominion, and

others, does not relate to the Transaction under review.71 As the Commission explained in the

Wolf Hills/Big Sandy Order, “arguments based on general concerns about certain elements of

PJM’s market design that are not specific to a proposed transaction under review are beyond the

scope of the Commission’s review of the proposed transaction,” and “[t]his proceeding, which

only concerns the Proposed Transactions, is not the appropriate venue for raising or addressing

general concerns regarding market design.” 72 Transactions by unaffiliated companies are
